claims.text: The proposed framework separately computes lattice thermal conductivity using disorder-corrected DFT phonon spectra and electronic thermal conductivity using DFT+Boltzmann transport.
The proposed framework will predict lattice thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr with roughly 30% lower error than Debye-based perfect-crystal analytical estimates.
Multi-element site occupancy in HfNbTaTiZr produces local variations in atomic masses and force constants.
Local force-constant disorder and mass fluctuations enhance phonon scattering.
The detailed electronic band structure governs the electronic contribution to heat transport.
Modeling lattice disorder, anharmonicity, and defect scattering enables the lattice and electronic heat-transport channels to be decoupled.
Assuming a perfect crystal and a single Debye temperature introduces predictive error for HfNbTaTiZr.
Below 200 K, HfNbTaTiZr has nearly equal lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.
From 300 to 1200 K, the predicted total thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr will be 10–17 W/(K m).
Measurements below 200 K indicate comparable lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr.
High-temperature measurements report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m) from 300 to 1200 K.
Earlier perfect-crystal DFT and Debye-based analytical approaches fail to capture disorder-induced phonon scattering.
Earlier approaches conflate or inaccurately estimate lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.
The model is applicable to defect-controlled or near-ideal HfNbTaTiZr samples with oxygen content no greater than 1 wt.%.
The model is applicable over approximately 50–1200 K.
Samples with significant extrinsic defects or oxygen levels much greater than 1 wt.% may lie outside the model's predictive range.
The estimated 30% improvement reflects typical shortcomings of Debye-based methods in disordered alloys.
Applying a magnetic field can suppress electronic heat transport sufficiently to help separate lattice and electronic contributions.
Time-domain thermoreflectance or transient grating spectroscopy can obtain separate temperature-dependent lattice and electronic conductivity data under the proposed conditions.
